_timing: No narration yet. Each beat is the larger of the time it needs to finish animating and the time it takes to read, plus a 22-frame hold. This is a floor, not considered pacing — measure a real read and switch this topic to voiceCuts.

beats.text: It was not a slip of the finger.
beats.note: Early accounts blamed a wrong button during a routine test. The employee's written statement says he mistakenly believed an exercise was a real event, after a drill call that included the words this is not a drill.

beats.name: Hawaii Emergency Management Agency
beats.role: At around 8:07 am on 13 January, phones across Hawaii read: BALLISTIC MISSILE THREAT INBOUND TO HAWAII. SEEK IMMEDIATE SHELTER. THIS IS NOT A DRILL.

beats.text: One person could send it alone.
beats.note: The FCC found that no second person had to approve an alert, and that test and live alerts shared one interface with an identical confirmation prompt.

beats.context: Until a correction reached phones through the alert system itself: There is no missile threat. False Alarm. A social media post had said so after 13 minutes. The agency had no procedure for correcting a false alert.

beats.text: Two people now approve every alert.
beats.note: Hawaii also added a cancellation command that works within seconds and a correction template. The agency's administrator, Vern Miyagi, resigned.
